quote: A numeric conversion requests another representation; this lesson demonstrates Double.toInt. Kotlin does not generally assign a numeric variable to another numeric type implicitly. Other conversion names, such as toLong and toDouble, are optional API references, not additional operations required here.

A numeric conversion requests another representation; this lesson demonstrates Double.toInt. Kotlin does not generally assign a numeric variable to another numeric type implicitly. Other conversion names, such as toLong and toDouble, are optional API references, not additional operations required here.
String values are immutable: building a different String does not rewrite the previous value. Case-conversion APIs such as uppercase are optional references beyond this interpolation example.

This lesson compares closed and half-open integer bounds. Stride selection with step and descending progressions with downTo are optional API references, not required by this example. A progression is not a promise of arbitrary floating-point steps.

In this separate worked call, also receives "sun" as its context value and exposes it as it. The lambda computes a length, but the whole also expression returns the original String; unlike let, it does not return that length.

Calling toMutableList on a list returns a new mutable outer list containing the same element references. Here adding to the copied container leaves the original container at one element; this is not a recursive clone.

The no-argument label call below has two different declared receiver types. The Base receiver returns "base" even though it holds a Detail object; the Detail receiver returns "detail". Neither extension overrides the other.

require(condition) throws IllegalArgumentException when an argument violates a precondition. The state-checking alternative check is only a comparison reference here; lesson 55 demonstrates its Boolean input, failure message and IllegalStateException behavior. Kotlin does not require checked-exception declarations on functions.

This complete failing-path companion constructs IllegalArgumentException with a diagnostic message and throws it inside use. The exception is not a normal return value: use closes the resource before the matching handler prints caught.

order.reversed() takes this comparator as receiver and returns a comparator with the entire ordering reversed. Passing it to sortedWith changes both the length ordering and equal-length lexical order without modifying the input list.
File("notes.txt") constructs an object representing that pathname; construction alone does not create or write the file. The later writeText call creates or replaces its contents.

Instant.parse takes ISO instant text such as "2025-01-01T00:30:00Z" and returns an Instant; Z identifies UTC. ZoneId.of takes a zone-ID String such as "UTC" or "America/New_York" and returns the corresponding ZoneId rules object. These are the inputs to the existing atZone calls.

A Job cancellation is a request, not a forced thread kill. Suspending library functions check cancellation; CPU-bound work must also cooperate. ensureActive is an optional reference for a later CPU-loop design, not an additional call required in this suspending handshake example. Do not swallow CancellationException as an ordinary successful result.

go build translates the program into an executable. The hands-on command below uses that build workflow. go run also builds before running, but is only a comparison here; lesson 41 gives its concrete module invocation. It is not an interpreter reading source statement by statement.
The initialized view below covers two elements, so len(view) returns 2, not the three-element owner length and not the last valid view index.
Error() takes the error value as receiver and returns its diagnostic message String. This direct call shows the message that fmt.Println(err) also displays for the simple error.

errors.Is tests whether an error matches a target, including through wrapping. Comparing strings is brittle. Typed extraction through errors.As is an optional further API reference, not a prerequisite for this sentinel-identity example or its quiz.

b.Fatalf takes the benchmark receiver, a format String and any formatting arguments. It records a benchmark failure and stops the current benchmark function. This is the benchmark counterpart of the earlier t.Fatalf test operation; the changed separator reaches this failure path.

Here Read receives a two-byte destination slice and returns how many bytes it filled plus an error. Write receives only those n bytes and returns how many it accepted plus an error. The explicit calls use an in-memory strings.Reader and bytes.Buffer; process returned bytes before interpreting a possible read error. The printed nil comparisons describe this particular successful read/write, not a promise that every Reader behaves identically.

file.WriteString("ready") writes the supplied String bytes to the open file and returns a byte count and an error. The underscore deliberately discards the count here; writeErr retains the failure result. It does not return the written String.

Store replaces one atomic integer with its supplied value; Load returns its current value. This sequential companion has no goroutines and is not a read-modify-write operation. Separate Load and Store calls would still not make an increment atomic.
w.Header() takes no arguments and returns the mutable header map associated with this pending response. Set updates that map; do so before committing status or body, not after the response has begun.

http.NotFound takes the response writer and request, writes status 404 and the standard "404 page not found" body with a newline. This recorder-only companion observes those effects directly; it opens no listener or socket.

io.ReadAll receives the response body as a Reader, consumes its remaining bytes and returns a byte slice plus an error. It can allocate for all remaining input, so this example deliberately supplies only its known tiny body.

request.Context() takes no arguments and returns the context attached to that request. Calling Err on that returned context observes whether cancellation or a deadline has already ended it; it does not create a new context.

text.chars() borrows the text and returns an iterator that yields Unicode scalar values. Calling count() on that iterator consumes it and returns the number of yielded scalars; it is not a byte-count or grapheme-segmentation operation.
values.len() takes the array as receiver and returns its element count. This array has three elements, whose valid indices stop at two.

A runtime invalid index panics; it does not extend the array. The checked get alternative is a reference for later: lesson 67 shows its index input and Option result. This example and quiz use only valid direct indices.
view.len() returns the element count of this borrowed range, not the length of the entire owner array. It borrows the slice without consuming or copying its elements.

HashMap<String, u32> owns its String keys. In the demonstrated entry(key) path, the map takes ownership of a supplied key when it inserts a new entry; lookup borrows a key instead. Direct insert is an optional API reference beyond this entry-based example. Hash-map iteration order is not a stable presentation order.
HashMap::new() creates an empty map. The type annotation or later uses determine its key and value types; constructing it does not prepopulate entries.
The no-argument len method returns the number of distinct stored entries. Here the repeated key updates one entry, so the map length is one; it is not the accumulated count stored at that key.
HashSet::new() creates an empty set. Subsequent insert calls let the compiler infer the element type; no values are added merely by construction.

This smaller formatting companion actually requests Display through the {} placeholder. fmt receives a shared error receiver and a borrowed mutable Formatter; write! sends the supplied message to that destination and returns the formatting Result, which fmt returns unchanged. It does not print independently of the caller.

RefCell::new(3) wraps that initial integer in a new RefCell; construction does not yet borrow the value. is_err() then takes the try_borrow_mut Result as receiver and returns true exactly when it is Err, without extracting its error payload.

RefCell::new(3) wraps that initial integer in a new RefCell; construction does not yet borrow the value. is_err() then takes the try_borrow_mut Result as receiver and returns true exactly when it is Err, without extracting its error payload.
Arc::clone(&value) receives a borrowed Arc and returns another strong owner of the same allocation. It does not copy the inner integer into a separate allocation.
is_some() takes the returned Option as receiver and reports whether it is Some. It does not extract the mutable reference or change the stored integer.
Mutex::new(3) constructs a new unlocked mutex containing the supplied integer. It is the later lock call that acquires guarded access.
AtomicUsize::new(0) constructs an atomic counter initialized to zero. Vec::new() creates an empty vector; pushing JoinHandles later determines its element type and grows its length.
AtomicUsize::new(0) constructs an atomic counter initialized to zero. Vec::new() creates an empty vector; pushing JoinHandles later determines its element type and grows its length.
count.load(Ordering::SeqCst) reads and returns the current atomic integer using the supplied ordering. It does not reset the counter; both joins finish before this observation.

store receives a replacement integer and an ordering, writes that value atomically and returns unit. This sequential companion demonstrates replacement, not a concurrent increment; a separate load followed by store would still be two operations.
input.as_bytes() borrows the UTF-8 bytes of the String slice as &[u8]. It does not allocate another String or change the input; Cursor receives that borrowed byte sequence.

io::Error::new takes an error kind and message and returns an io::Error value. The invalid helper chooses InvalidData and the supplied message; constructing the error does not throw it, and Err/? control its propagation.
args.as_slice() borrows all elements of the argument vector as a slice. It neither consumes the vector nor copies its Strings; the slice pattern can inspect the borrowed length and entries.

std::env::args yields Unicode command-line argument Strings. skip(1) omits the conventional program-name entry, then collect::<Vec<String>> stores the user arguments. args can panic on invalid Unicode. The args_os alternative for operating-system strings is an explicitly deferred platform-boundary reference; this worked invocation and its quiz use Unicode arguments only.

isset checks whether the supplied entry is both present and non-null. array_key_exists receives a key and array and tests key presence even when the stored value is null. Both return Booleans; neither modifies the array. This concrete comparison keeps a present zero distinct from null.

Status::from takes a backing value and returns the matching case, but throws ValueError for an unknown value of the valid scalar type. The companion handles that failure explicitly; unlike tryFrom, from does not return null for it.

With the same trusted helper.php shown above beside this companion, plain require evaluates that file each time. Its input is the explicit local path; its observable effect here is two output lines, unlike require_once.

require evaluates the target PHP file; an unavailable required file causes an Error. The include warning/false alternative is a reference only, not an additional hands-on operation here. Use explicit trusted paths, never user input as executable include paths.

PHP invokes __clone on the new outer object after copying its properties. This no-argument hook replaces that copy’s nested Note with a cloned Note; $this is the new Box. It returns no value. The later edit therefore no longer changes first.note.
This explicit alternate call creates a Closure for plusOne without invoking it immediately. apply supplies integer 4 to that callable; plusOne returns 5, which apply then returns to echo.

Passing Label::class to getAttributes filters the returned descriptors to that known attribute class. The argument is a class-name String, not a request to instantiate the attribute; newInstance performs construction separately.

getNumberOfParameters takes a reflected method as receiver and returns its declared parameter count, including optional parameters. It does not invoke the method. This known local method has one parameter.

The explicit sort call below receives the mutable array and numeric-comparison flag. It changes that array in place and reindexes its entries to 0 and 1; the returned success Boolean is not the sorted array.

ksort orders the keys in place while keeping each value attached. Here SORT_STRING compares the supplied String keys lexically; the call returns success rather than a replacement array. This differs from sorting values with sort or asort.

extension_loaded("mbstring") receives an extension-name String and returns a Boolean indicating whether that extension is loaded in this process. The guard rejects an unavailable extension rather than changing the meaning of the length operation.

The DateTimeImmutable constructor receives timestamp text and a DateTimeZone object and returns a new immutable date-time object. Because this timestamp text contains no zone of its own, the explicit UTC object supplies its interpretation; the constructor does not read the current time here.

exit(0) ends this CLI process immediately with success status zero; statements after it do not run. Running the existing main.php with no user argument reaches that call and prints only "usage: php main.php MINUTES". This is process behavior, not a browser-response test.

ErrorException receives message, numeric code, severity, source filename and source line in that order. The code argument is 0 here; the other values come from the handler callback. Construction returns the throwable object, and throw transfers control to catch.

min(10, $n) returns the smaller supplied number, imposing the upper bound. max(0, thatResult) returns the larger supplied number, imposing the lower bound. These return numbers without modifying $n; for $n = 11 the inner result is 10 and the outer result stays 10.

urlencode receives this component String and returns its form-style encoded String. It does not send a request or change the original value; the space becomes + while the slash is still percent-encoded.

http_build_query receives the data map, an empty numeric-key prefix (unused by these String keys), the pair separator "&", and PHP_QUERY_RFC3986 to choose percent-encoded spaces. It returns a query String, not a full URL or network response.

PASSWORD_DEFAULT can evolve over PHP releases. Real storage must accommodate future hash lengths and a deliberate rehash policy; password_needs_rehash is an explicitly deferred production-authentication API reference, not a call required by this verification example. This synthetic fixture is not a complete login system: rate limiting, account isolation and transport security remain separate requirements.

is_dir(path) returns whether the supplied path names a directory. mkdir(path, 0700) attempts directory creation and returns success/failure; permissions are affected by the process umask and platform, so this is not a portable sandbox guarantee. ini_set(name, value) changes a configurable directive for this process and returns its previous value or false on failure. session_save_path(directory) selects file-session storage before starting the session and returns the previous path (or false on failure); setting it alone does not create the directory.

session_id() without an argument reads the current identifier; session_id($id) selects that identifier before the next session_start. session_destroy() destroys the stored data for the active session and returns success/failure, but does not automatically erase the in-memory $_SESSION array or delete a browser cookie. Those are separate responsibilities in a real web application.

The cookie-configuration API session_set_cookie_params is deferred to a real cookie-enabled web integration. Such an integration must choose Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite settings before starting the session, then verify actual Set-Cookie and browser behavior; this cookie-disabled CLI example does not demonstrate that API.

This isolated array-only companion shows unset removing the specified key without ending a session or destroying other data. Its input is the selected entry, and the null-coalescing read then uses the missing-key fallback. The session fixture separately verifies saving and reopening that deletion.

PDO::getAvailableDrivers() takes no arguments and returns an array of driver-name Strings loaded in this PHP process; the strict in_array check looks for "sqlite". In the second SELECT, SQL COUNT(*) returns the number of selected rows, and fetchColumn reads that single result column. It is a database aggregate, not a PHP function.

array_sum($accepted) takes the array and returns the numeric sum of its entries. In this fixture every entry is already a validated integer, so the returned total is the bounded integer sum rather than a count of entries.
